steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high‐level, conceptual overview of how a Transformer works:

1. Tokenization & Embedding  
   • Input text is split into tokens (words, subwords, or bytes).  
   • Each token is mapped to a learned vector (an embedding).  
   • Positional encodings are added so the model knows the order of tokens.

2. Self-Attention Mechanism  
   • For each token embedding, three vectors are computed by learned linear projections: Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V).  
   • Attention scores are computed by taking the dot product Q·Kᵀ (for each token pair), then scaling and applying softmax.  
   • Each token’s new representation is a weighted sum of all Value vectors, where weights come from those softmaxed scores.  
   • This lets every token “attend” to others, capturing dependencies regardless of distance.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Instead of one Q/K/V projection, the model learns several (“heads”) in parallel.  
   • Each head attends to different aspects of the sequence.  
   • The heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

4. Add & Norm  
   • A residual (skip) connection adds the attention output to the original embeddings.  
   • Layer normalization stabilizes and speeds up training.

5. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
   • Each token representation passes through the same small two-layer feed-forward network (with nonlinearity, e.g. ReLU).  
   • Another residual connection + layer norm follows.

6. Stacking Layers  
   • Steps 2–5 form one Transformer block.  
   • Many such blocks are stacked (e.g. 6–48 layers), allowing deep feature extraction.

7. Encoder vs. Decoder  
   • In encoder-only models (like BERT), you keep just the stack above.  
   • In encoder–decoder models (like original “Transformer” for translation), the decoder stack additionally:  
     – Masks self-attention so each position can only attend to earlier positions (for autoregressive generation).  
     – Cross-attention layers where decoder queries attend to encoder outputs.

8. Output & Prediction  
   • For tasks like language modeling, the final decoder layer projects each position back to the token-vocabulary size and applies softmax to predict next tokens.  
   • For classification or tagging, a special token (e.g. [CLS]) or per-token outputs are fed into task-specific heads.

Key takeaway:  
Transformers replace recurrence and convolutions with global self-attention, letting every position flexibly incorporate information from any other. Deep stacks of attention + feed-forward blocks, with residual connections and normalization, let them learn rich representations for a wide variety of language tasks.
